title: LLM Value Functions for Credit Assignment in Agentic RL
authors: Kaijie Zhu, Weixiang Yan, Omar Attia et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) agents remains challenging in long-horizon tasks with sparse outcome rewards, where assigning credit to individual actions is difficult. Methods such as GRPO assign the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, while critic-based methods require learning an additional value function that can be costly and unstable. title: Agent Sociodrama: Social-Dynamics-Guided Persona Recasting for LLM Agent Teams
authors: Yirui Qi, Xiaoming Zhang, Jaehong Yoon
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as teams, yet they fail in characteristically social ways: information holders stay silent, dominant speakers anchor groups on wrong answers, and norm violations go unsanctioned. We present Agent Sociodrama, a framework for modeling and validating evolving social dynamics in LLM agent teams. Under fixed personas, agents' emotional states and directed, asymmetric relationships are updated every round by a unified external LLM judge and s

title: SurgiCLAW: An Interpretable Atomic-Skill Agent for Precision Robotic Micromanipulation
authors: Angen Ye, junjie xie, Yujia Song et al.
abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and vision--language--action models have provided robots with new capabilities for long-horizon task understanding and planning. In surgical robotics, however, end-to-end prediction of low-level actions remains limited by insufficient precision, opaque decisions, and scarce data. title: A Decade in a Day: Synthesizing Agent-Native Interfaces from Human-Oriented Software Evolution
authors: Alan Wu, Wei Tao, Yiwen Guo
abstract: Large language model agents are emerging as an important new class of users of desktop applications. However, existing desktop interfaces were designed for human end users or application developers, leaving agents to interpret visual controls or discover and compose low-level software operations. This mismatch can hinder even capable agents, yet it remains unclear what interface properties make desktop software easier for agents to use. title: Agent-Canary-Mas: End-to-End Evaluation of Protocol Risk in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Xiuming Liu, Le Gai, Zhiyuan Chang et al.
abstract: Agent-to-agent protocols allow LLM agents to discover peers, exchange results, and coordinate tool use. A locally successful protocol attack, however, may be rejected by a later agent or propagated into a consequential task decision. Measuring local exploitability alone leaves this difference unresolved and provides limited evidence about which participant caused the final outcome. title: When Skills Remain But Access Fails: Factorized Skill Memory for Continual Skill Internalization
authors: Haomiao Qiu, Yining Tang, Hongyi Wan et al.
abstract: Skill internalization aims to convert externally specified procedural skills into persistent model capabilities, allowing language-model agents to execute them without retrieving or reinjecting skill descriptions at inference time. Yet when new skills are learned continually, whether previously internalized skills remain usable is still poorly understood. We study forgetting in continual skill internalization and uncover a clear hierarchical structure. Early in subsequent training, a model may l

title: AlphaPilot: Multi-Turn Tool-Using LLM Agents for Adaptive Alpha Mining with Reinforcement Learning
authors: Peiqi Jiang, Fan Zhang, Xin Xu et al.
abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks interpretable expressions that rank assets by future returns. The task is challenging because it demands simultaneous processing of unstructured market descriptions, historical data, and quantitative evaluation of candidate factors, yet most existing methods exploit only a subset of these signals. We introduce AlphaPilot, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains multi-turn tool-using LLM agents for adaptive alpha mining. The agent conditions on market descripti

title: SkillFusion: Towards Reliable Multi-Skill Composition for LLM Agents
authors: Enhao Huang, Xinye Zhao, Yiming Li et al.
abstract: Independently authored skills can impose incompatible requirements, competing preferences, and redundant instructions when jointly loaded by an LLM agent. We propose SkillFusion, an offline compiler that reconciles these interactions into a reusable merged skill. Its central idea is to make composition decisions explicit through typed, scoped constraints linked to their source directives. title: Sequent-Prover: Training Agents for Formal, Checkable SMT-based Reasoning
authors: Debargha Ganguly, Weicong Chen, Mohsen Hariri et al.
abstract: We introduce Sequent-Prover, a family of verifier-using language-model agents, and the post-training framework that produces them. Agents reason in an executable SMT-LIB scratchpad: they write complete SMT-LIB programs, query Z3 across turns, inspect solver feedback, repair formalizations, and terminate with an explicit answer. title: Unfair and Unsafe: Everyday Bias Triggers Emergent Misalignment
authors: Alex Martí Guiu, Nicolas Zumarraga, Kevin O'Sullivan et al.
abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) occurs when fine-tuning a language model to a narrow task makes it misaligned on unrelated ones. Because organizations now routinely fine-tune models on their own data, it matters which kinds of training data cause EM. So far, studies have induced EM with data containing recognized safety failures, such as insecure code or harmful advice, while biased training data is typically examined by fairness research for the bias models learn from it rather than for its effects

title: More Reasoning Is Not Always Better: Executing Clinical Guidelines with LLMs and Rules
authors: Xiaoqian Lu, Guangfu Guo, Long Cheng et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in clinical decision support. However, existing approaches often rely on multi-step reasoning or multi-agent collaboration to execute clinical guidelines, introducing substantial computational overhead without reliably preventing decision errors. title: Adaptive Look, Flexible Thought: Learning How and How Long to Think in Multimodal Reasoning
authors: Quanlin Chen, Xiuwei Chen, Kun Xiang et al.
abstract: The introduction of long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and external tools has substantially improved the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on general and reasoning tasks. However, existing fast-slow reasoning paradigms mainly regulate textual reasoning length, while visual computation introduced by external tools or visual tokens is often treated as an auxiliary component. This separation prevents MLLMs from jointly optimizing visual perception and textual reasoning. To

title: TL;QR: Querying Temporal Discursive Patterns in Textual Corpora
authors: François Hublet, Vladimir Krsmanovic, Jesus Solano et al.
abstract: Many questions about large textual corpora concern patterns that unfold over time, such as a political group whose stance on a topic drifts from support to criticism over several years of debates. We present TL;QR (Too Long; Query with logical temporal Reasoning), a declarative query language and open-source engine for finding such temporal discursive patterns. title: Knowledge Interaction in Hypernetwork-based Continual Learning: Conflict and Composition
authors: Jiaqi Zheng, Yi Hu, Yadong Mu et al.
abstract: Continual learning aims to adapt pretrained large language models (LLMs) to evolving data while preserving their pretrained capabilities. A central challenge is catastrophic forgetting: adaptation to new data can impair performance on previously learned knowledge. Since continual learning commonly changes model parameters, the model's predictions may draw on knowledge from the base model, the parameter update, and the input context. title: A Persian Vision-Language-Action Dataset and Benchmark for Ambiguity- and Infeasibility-Aware Instruction-to-Plan Grounding
authors: Abdollah Pourasghari, Saeedeh Sadat Sadidpour, Mohammad Roustaei
abstract: Converting natural-language instructions into executable action plans conditioned on a scene image is a core capability for embodied human-robot interaction, but existing benchmarks target English, simulated or video-grounded environments, and largely assume instructions are clear and executable. title: From Stages to States: Unified Iterative Reasoning for MLLMs
authors: Chuang Yu, Xuefei Ma, Yuanhao Feng et al.
abstract: Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) substantially enhances the complex reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by explicitly modeling intermediate reasoning processes. However, most learning-based MCoT methods follow a stage-centric paradigm, where different reasoning behaviors are assigned to predefined stages and optimized separately. title: The Fragility and Dynamics of LLM Pruning-Recovery Steps
authors: Luis Frentzen Salim, Komang Rinartha, Chia-Chun Wu et al.
abstract: Structural pruning followed by a recovery stage is the standard recipe for compressing large language models (LLMs), yet the two stages are typically designed and tuned in isolation. In this work, we study how their interaction shapes the compressed model, sweeping ordering, the data that drives each stage, and the alignment of their training objectives. title: Large Decision Models: Repurposing Large Language Models as Single-Pass Decision Makers
authors: Ziyi Chen, Yan Zhang, Jianhui Wei et al.
abstract: Large language models make decisions through parallel prefill and sequential decoding. Although effective, this approach incurs decoding costs and does not explicitly expose decision probabilities. Existing task-specific classifiers require per-task training and offer limited generalization to unseen decision schemas. title: Do correct answers have stable latent knowledge support?
authors: Chuancheng Shi, Shangze Li, Wenhua Wu et al.
abstract: Large language models are typically evaluated in terms of the correctness of their output. However, output correctness alone does not confirm whether the latent knowledge supporting an answer has stable internal representations. We therefore propose latent state stability (LSS) and knowledge topology stability (KTS) to investigate the stability of individual knowledge states and their relational structure, respectively. title: RECAP: Calibrating Low-Bit Reasoning Models on the History They Read
authors: Chi Ruan, Yujie Chen, Zixiang Zhao et al.
abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the cost of serving reasoning models but can substantially degrade long chains of thought. Each step reads cached keys and values spanning thousands of tokens, allowing quantization errors to accumulate along the trajectory. Standard calibration operates on short segments that omit the earlier context needed by later reasoning steps. title: ClinEdge: An Expert-Graded Benchmark of Real Patient Edge Cases Where Frontier Multimodal Models Fail
authors: Anurag Sharma, Aditya Sharma, Sapna Baalwan
abstract: Most benchmarks for large language models in medicine are built from licensing examinations and theoretical questions. The few that draw on real clinical data do so only in part, and rarely require a model to read a patient's own imaging. ClinEdge addresses this gap with 32 real, de-identified patient cases from active clinical practice, each evaluated across seven frontier systems for a total of 224 expert-graded evaluations. title: Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners
authors: Project Apertus,  :, Yixuan Xu et al.
abstract: Language models are becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure built in the open, by public institutions, on documented data, is the alternative to dependence on a few providers; Apertus shows this is viable at scale. Apertus 1.5 extends the fully open Apertus family from text to multimodal reasoning. Continued pretraining of the Apertus 1.0 models, on 4T additional tokens for the 8B and 2T for the 70B, adds image and audio understanding and extends the context window fourfold to 262,144 tokens

title: Engram Injection: A Study of Temporal Validity in Parametric Language-Model Memory
authors: Sam Siavoshian, Omar Ramadan, Amir K. Saeed et al.
abstract: A stored fact may stop being valid when a user changes a preference or an event replaces an earlier one. We study whether a language model can learn these changes in its parameters and answer correctly from only a question and the current time. Engram Injection stores facts in LoRA adapters and supplies the clock through FiLM conditioning on a frozen Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model. title: Personalized LLM Recommendation with Semantic IDs: Autoregressive Beam Search vs. Multi-Token Prediction
authors: Sejoon Oh, Fernando Amat Gil, Evan Smothers et al.
abstract: Large-scale personalization is shifting from embedding-table retrieval to LLM-based recommenders that generate the Semantic ID (SID) of the item to recommend, where each SID is a short sequence of discrete hierarchical content codes. A single instruction-tuned model can then unify retrieval, content understanding, and language, and recommend brand-new titles from their content alone using SID; then, how should the model generate the SID? title: Large language model-generated patterns for epidemiological modeling: a multi-benchmark evaluation framework
authors: Sophia Mao, Keshav Gandhi, Alexander Gutfraind
abstract: Representing individual-level behavioral heterogeneity is challenging in epidemiological modeling, particularly when empirical behavioral data are sparse. We assess the potential of large language model (LLM)-generated behavioral outputs in addressing this challenge, using hepatitis C virus-related behaviors among people who inject drugs as a case study. Correspondence with epidemiological patterns was evaluated using external benchmarks: literature-informed association directions, correlations

title: Attention Sinks in VLMs Are Borrowed, Not Seen
authors: Dengjia Zhang, Alexander Martin, Pengyu Yan et al.
abstract: We study how to detect and mitigate visual attention sinks in vision-language models (VLMs). Visual attention sinks are image tokens that absorb a large share of attention over the image regardless of the query or task, and they mislead methods that treat attention maps as a record of where the model ``looked.'' title: Latent Taxonomies: How Property Induction Develops in Language Model Pre-training
authors: Jan Sobotka, Ekaterina Goliakova, Marcin Detyniecki et al.
abstract: When told that robins have sesamoid bones, people are far more prone to extend the property to sparrows than to whales. This behavior, called category-based property induction, is well documented in humans, but whether and how it develops in language models trained only to predict the next token is unclear. title: NepPlural: A Human-Anchored Benchmark for Persona Annotation in Nepali Migration Discourse
authors: Jinu Nyachhyon, Anish Khatiwada, Bimal Timilsina
abstract: Pluralistic alignment asks that language models faithfully represent a society's diverse, competing values rather than collapse them into one dominant viewpoint, yet flagship pluralistic-alignment datasets remain heavily skewed toward Western respondents. We introduce NepPlural, a human-anchored benchmark for modelling competing socio-cultural personas in Nepali public discourse on youth migration and brain drain. title: REPRO: Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimizer for Automated LLM Red-Teaming
authors: Abrar Alotaibi, Moataz Ahmed
abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that bypass their safety training. Existing automated red-teaming methods either require privileged access unavailable in production, rely on manually engineered per-model templates, or optimize a single objective without population-level diversity. title: North or South? Diagnosing LLMs' Understanding of North Korean Language, Society, and Knowledge
authors: Kiwoong Park, Seyoung Song, Donghyun Woo et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in multilingual question answering, yet their ability to understand low-resource sociolinguistic contexts remains under-explored. We study North Korea as a unique testbed where decades of division have produced distinct differences from South Korea in vocabulary, orthography, norms, and ideological discourse. We introduce LENS (Language and sociocultural Evaluation for North Korean Society), a human-validated benchmark of 1,765 question

title: MoMaTune: Model, Match, Then Tune Language Models for Numerical Records
authors: Weimin Lyu, Jingfen Zhang, Lingdao Sha et al.
abstract: Despite remarkable progress in language understanding and generation, decoder language models continue to exhibit striking failures on numerical data. Numerical examples are typically serialized as text by concatenating feature names with their values (e.g., fat:3.4), while conventional task adaptation applies loss only to the downstream prediction target. title: In-Place Indic Tokenizer Expansion and Continual Pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B
authors: Avinash Benki, Prasanjith Pasunuti, Sutanshu Saksena Raj et al.
abstract: We adapted Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B for eight Indian languages without changing its backbone architecture. We expanded the vocabulary in place from 131,072 to 163,072 entries using continued byte-pair encoding and AdaptMix rebalancing, reducing tokens per word by 38.6%. We initialized new input and output rows by averaging their original constituent rows, then trained them on 90% Indic and 10% English text before updating the backbone. title: Handoff Curves: Initial Selection, Later Handoff, and Supervision Targets in Multi-turn LLM Routing
authors: Daniel Matos, Lu Liu, Yanfeng Zhang
abstract: We study how initial model selection, later handoff, and training targets affect success and cost in LLM tasks that span multiple turns. We compare several router architectures using handoff curves, which record task success and cost as the handoff step changes. Our dataset contains 34,204 complete executions of three Qwen models across BFCL, MultiWOZ, and $τ$-retail, providing offline supervision for routing decisions. title: PopGen: Generating Semantically Diverse Populations for Zero-Shot Coordination
authors: Paul Teiletche, Kanghyun Ryu, Kyungjoon Park et al.
abstract: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, exposing a cooperator to partners with diverse strategies during training is key to better collaboration at test time. However, existing methods typically rely on trajectory-level proxies to measure diversity, which may label two distinct trajectories of the same strategy as diverse. title: What the Model Cannot See: Covert and Provable Text Invisibility in LLMs
authors: Mark Russinovich
abstract: Text wrapped in a trigger can be made behaviorally invisible to a language model: omitted from summaries and quotations, ignored in question answering, and left unflagged by downstream filtering. We study this selective blindness as a dual-use information-flow primitive, a supply-chain backdoor, and a white-box auditing problem. title: Google Earth AI Geospatial Reasoning Agent: Capabilities and a Systematic Evaluation
authors: Noam Slonim, Aviv Slobodkin, Gil Fidel et al.
abstract: Google Earth AI is a family of geospatial AI models, together with an agent that orchestrates them. We present this agent, Google Earth AI's Geospatial Reasoning agent (GRA), a Gemini-powered research system that combines geospatial data sources, foundation models, and tools to answer questions about our planet. title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Advancing Harmful Content Understanding via Perception-Aware Adversarial Self-Play
authors: Yisong Xiao, Benlei Cui, Shiji Zhao et al.
abstract: Despite significant advances in language understanding, Large Language Models (LLMs) can still miss meaning hidden in plain sight, failing to identify harmful intent in expressions readily understood by humans. Malicious users exploit this gap by strategically disguising harmful content to evade automated moderation, posing a serious threat to online platform safety. title: GA-SVD: Generation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for LLM Compression
authors: Shengkun Tang, Cong Zeng, Zongfang Liu et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong generalization across a broad range of reasoning and generation tasks, but their large parameter counts impose substantial memory and computation costs, hindering deployment in practical resource-constrained settings. One-shot low-rank compression is a promising solution since it reduces model size and inference cost effectively. title: SAFE-KV: Causal Suffix Repair for Behavior-Preserving Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in RAG
authors: Xingjian Zhang
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reuses the same documents across many requests, making non-prefix KV-cache reuse attractive. Yet a cached document state is not reusable text: it is a context-conditioned causal state whose keys and values depend on the prefix, position, and preceding documents under which it was computed. title: Training-Free BioNEL-RAG: Advancing Biomedical Entity Linking through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Large Language Model
authors: Ziyi Chen, Hui Liu, Ziyang Ling et al.
abstract: Biomedical Named Entity Linking (BioNEL) is the task of mapping mentions extracted from biomedical texts to canonical entities or concepts in the standardized knowledge base. Although existing methods have achieved remarkable performance in mapping accuracy, most rely on training with domain-specific datasets, which fundamentally limits their cross-domain adaptability. To address this limitation, we propose BioNEL-RAG, a novel training-free framework that combines retrieval-augmented generation

title: LongHisDoc: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chinese Long Historical Document Understanding
authors: Zeyu Shan, Yongxin Shi, Shihang Wu et al.
abstract: Chinese historical documents are invaluable cultural treasures, but their complexity poses significant comprehension challenges for non-specialists. Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) in modern document tasks, their capabilities in Long (full-book) Historical Document understanding remain largely unexplored. title: Frustratingly Easy Agentic RAG via Portable Skills: A Case Study in Customer Support
authors: Istok Bako, Bonan Min, Tiffany Shao et al.
abstract: Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. title: Harmony Harness: Multi-Objective Self-Evolution of Agent Harnesses
authors: Weichen Yu, Lesly Miculicich, Bhavana Dalvi Mishra et al.
abstract: Recent work on self-evolving LLM agents treats the agent harness as an optimization target that can be iteratively improved through execution feedback. Existing approaches, however, largely optimize a single objective and evolve the harness as a monolithic artifact, limiting their ability to handle competing goals and to separate transferable design from environment-specific adaptation. title: Beyond Outcome Feedback: Trajectory-Quality-Guided Experience-based Learning
authors: Bingjie Zhang, Yibo Yang, Qiantong Liu et al.
abstract: Experience-based learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve over time by reusing knowledge from past executions. However, existing methods typically rely on final task outcomes as feedback for experience learning, overlooking the execution process and limiting their ability to evaluate and optimize experience based on trajectory quality. title: PEAM: On-device Communication Agent for Personalized, Efficient and Autonomous Mobile Network Configuration
authors: Haowen Wan, Shangzhuo Xie, Syue-Ju Syue et al.
abstract: The growing deployment of compact large language models on smartphones is enabling autonomous on-device decision-making, such as emerging mobile GUI agents. However, many mobile decisions, such as network configuration when users switch apps or connectivity conditions change, must satisfy stringent latency constraints to preserve user experience. title: Think in Strategies, Act with Tools: Traceable Agentic Optimization for Combinatorial Problems
authors: Zhongnian Li, Shi Xu, Peng Ying et al.
abstract: Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) directly leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate candidate solutions through natural-language prompting. However, OPRO's optimization process is difficult to track, which prevents LLMs from capturing useful information accumulated over previous iterations, thereby limiting solution quality. title: Limitations on Autoregressive Token Generation via Sequential Sampling
authors: Gal Arnon, Andrej Bogdanov, Paul Lou et al.
abstract: We study autoregressive token generation through the notion of sequential samplers: A circuit that samples the next symbol only given the previous ones and possibly a small amount of state. title: CB-Agent: Concept-Based In-Context Learning for Sequential Action Selection
authors: Qingyue Zhang, Huaze Tang, Minyu Zhang et al.
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows large language models to use demonstrations without updating their parameters. For interactive agents, demonstrations are trajectories of reasoning, actions, and observations that illustrate how to complete a task. title: Re-executing Coding-Agent Evaluations: Unchanged Decisions and Unresolved Policy Risk
authors: Tianyu Ding, Yaocheng Tong, Muzhi Yang et al.
abstract: Executable tests grade large language model (LLM) coding-agent patches for leaderboards, rewards and self-improvement. Two preregistered re-execution studies returned negative results. SWE-bench Pro v1's offline option rejected none of 59 accepted Go patches whose grading configuration changed. title: MemForm: Benchmarking Memory Formation Poisoning in LLM Agents
authors: Haowen Pan, Pengyang Shao, Yunshan Ma et al.
abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to learn from past interactions but exposes memory formation to adversarial influence. Existing studies primarily organize memory poisoning by attack channels, corruption patterns, or lifecycle stages, leaving formation interfaces insufficiently characterized. title: MCPDisCo: Seesaw-Mitigated Tuning for MCP-Native Agents
authors: Kounianhua Du, Jianxing Liu, Shuai Shao et al.
abstract: The Model Context Protocol provides a shared interaction substrate for the agentic web, allowing heterogeneous services to expose capabilities through a standardized interface. Learning to use this ecosystem entails a hierarchy of capabilities: tool-format skills, server-level transfer, and cross-server composition. title: SAGE: Pushing 2-Bit Vector-Quantized LLMs toward Real-World Usability
authors: Xianglong Yan, Zenan Wu, Kewei Zhang et al.
abstract: Extreme low-bit weight-only quantization is an effective approach to reducing the deployment costs of large language models. Below 3 bits, scalar quantization often suffers severe accuracy loss, while vector quantization (VQ) better preserves accuracy through more expressive joint encoding. title: Words to World: Benchmarking LLMs in Interactive Physical Environments
authors: Xinnan Dai, Kaiqi Yang, Yaxin Li et al.
abstract: Words are increasingly becoming an interface for action: large language models (LLMs) can now invoke tools, operate devices, and make decisions that affect the physical world. However, current benchmarks largely evaluate LLMs through static text responses, offline tool calls, or simulated tasks, leaving open the question of how well they can act in real physical environments. title: UDHRBench: Benchmarking Human Rights in Large Language Models
authors: Alak Raad, Noreldin Morssy, Zeerak Suhail et al.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. title: Where Did We Go Wrong? Localizing Errors to Repair Multi-Turn Conversations
authors: Alessandro Morosini, Wei Sun, Georgia Perakis
abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants are increasingly used in multi-turn conversations, where the user's intent is often unclear at first and revealed only gradually over time. The assistant must therefore interpret each exchange and form inferences about the user's intent, using them to update its working state. title: Lumen-bench: Cross-Lingual Safety Gaps and the Say-Do Problem in Tool-Calling Large Language Models
authors: Giovana Kerche Bonás, Thiago Laitz, Thales Sales Almeida et al.
abstract: When a large language model refuses an unethical request, what does refusal mean? In conversation, refusal is bounded by what the model says; once the model is equipped with executable tools, what it does can diverge from what it says, a failure mode that English-only evaluations cannot fully reveal. title: Structural Chain-of-Thought: Reasoning with Executable Computational Graphs
authors: Petr Senatorov, Karim Vafin, Elena Tutubalina et al.
abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting enables reasoning in large language models but produces explanations that are difficult to verify, expensive to generate, and not always faithful. We introduce a Structural Chain-of-Thought framework where models generate executable computational graphs instead of free-form reasoning. title: Lingdan-V2: Large language models for clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine
authors: Rui Hua, Yu Wei, Ziri Jin et al.
abstract: Large language models have advanced medical reasoning, but clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) remains challenging because prescription decisions require integrating domain knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, herbal prescription composition, and dosage determination. title: PVFH-Bench: Benchmarking Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models
authors: Xinhao Wang, Junbo Cui, Zhenghao Liu et al.
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across a wide range of multimodal tasks. However, object hallucination remains a persistent challenge, undermining model reliability in applications such as visual question answering, embodied agents, and human-AI decision support systems. title: Reward-Aligned Distillation
authors: Yilan Chen, Zian Su, Manish Prajapat et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but remains computationally expensive and sample inefficient. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, yet standard OPD distills every token regardless of whether the teacher's preference actually improves task reward. title: PsyMemBehav: Psychology-Informed and Memory-Grounded Two-Level Identity-to-Action Reasoning for Social-Media Behavior Simulation
authors: Wenji Zhang, Xilong Cheng, Yunxiao Qin et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support social simulation, but faithfully reproducing real users requires grounding both structured platform decisions and language in sparse, noisy behavioral evidence. We introduce PsyMemBehav, which maps psychology-informed profiles and retrieved memories to target-first platform behavior through two-level identity-to-action reasoning. title: GG-Nav: Goal-oriented Grounding Chain-of-Thought Elicits Reasoning in Navigation Foundation Models
authors: Shaohao Zhu, Wensi Huang, Siqi Zhang et al.
abstract: Emerging strong Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have advanced navigation foundation models. However, these models still have unsatisfactory performance on goal-oriented navigation settings. In this paper, we first conduct a motivating study revealing that the key issue lies in the insufficient utilization of streaming observations and imprecise target localization. title: Query-Adaptive Neuron Steering for LLMs
authors: Yanxi Pan, Jingwen Wu, Yan Ma et al.
abstract: Effectively eliciting the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) at inference time remains an important challenge. Existing studies address this challenge through context engineering, which shapes user queries, or fixed steering, which directly intervenes in model computation. However, predefined contexts and fixed intervention strategies may not adequately accommodate the diverse knowledge and reasoning requirements of individual queries. title: Target-ESS Tempered Policy Optimization (TETPO): Smooth Variance Control via Bridge Importance Sampling
authors: Shayan Mohajer Hamidi, Kayhan Behdin, Wenhui Zhu et al.
abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement-learning post-training of large language models is computationally efficient but inherently off-policy: the learner updates on rollouts generated by a stale policy, while correcting this mismatch requires importance weights that can be extremely heavy-tailed. A small number of trajectories may then dominate an update, collapsing the effective sample size (ESS) and increasing the variance and instability of the resulting gradient estimates. title: Neither True nor False: Do LLMs Represent Truth-Value Gaps in Plural Predication?
authors: Duaa Nakshbandi, Zhiyu An, Yiping Li et al.
abstract: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) genuinely grasp the truth conditions of plural descriptions, or do they force every sentence into true or false? We investigate the Homogeneity Gap, a semantic phenomenon where a plural definite (e.g., the kids laughed) and its negation (the kids didn't laugh) are both neither true nor false when only some of the kids laughed, whereas their quantified counterparts (all, not all) remain strictly bivalent. title: Understanding Unified VLMs: From Attention Probing to Guidance Tuning for Multimodal Generation
authors: Zhengyang Luo, Xiaoyu Qiu, Zhiheng Tan et al.
abstract: Unified vision-language models (VLMs) perform both text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) generation with one shared Transformer backbone, yet how the backbone processes the condition in either direction remains poorly understood. We study this question from the perspective of conditional guidance: we probe every attention head to show the activation difference between two branches of classifier-free guidance (CFG) with different conditional guidance. title: GesBench: When and Where Do Multimodal Language Models Perceive Social Meaning?
authors: Zonghuan Li, Hayley Hung, Chirag Raman
abstract: Human social perception is incremental: we infer intent before an utterance is complete, revise our interpretation as new cues arrive, and attend to specific facial, gestural, or prosodic signals that shape social meaning. Current multimodal LLM benchmarks largely evaluate final-answer understanding over complete episodes, rewarding post-hoc recognition of social meaning rather than the unfolding perception required for real-time interaction. title: CUSE: Fine-Grained Multimodal Unlearning with Counterfactual Guidance and On-Policy Self-Distillation
authors: Chenlu Ding, Jiancan Wu, Yanchen Luo et al.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reproduce sensitive, copyrighted, or unsafe information from their training data. Effective unlearning must remove target information while preserving non-target content, even within the same response. Existing methods typically apply uniform forgetting objectives to complete responses and rely on fixed, off-policy supervision, resulting in coarse token control and misalignment with the model's current behavior. title: Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures
authors: Aditi Khandelwal, Ayush K. Tarun, Yixuan Xu et al.
abstract: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. title: Toward System One Clinical Intelligence: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Counterfactual Explainability of Decision Foundation Models
authors: S. M. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed
abstract: Automated disease classification from patient-reported symptoms requires balancing the speed of lightweight discriminative models against the contextual understanding and latency costs of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Decision foundation models offer an alternative by mapping representations directly to candidate classes without free-form text generation. title: HiPAD: A Unified Gait, Audio-Visual, and Personality Fusion Network for Depression Detection, with a Hierarchical Personality Ablation and the Calibration Limits of Domain-Adapted LLMs
authors: Karol Chlasta, Piotr Struzik
abstract: We present HiPAD, a single fusion network submitted to all six sub-tracks of the MPDD-AVG 2026 depression-detection challenge, covering the Elder and Young cohorts and three modality sets (gait, audio-visual, and both), each combined with personality descriptions. The network encodes each available modality with a shared BiLSTM, zero-pads absent modalities, and applies cross-modal attention only when at least two of gait, audio and video are present. title: AcrossVAM2.0: Conflict-Aware Point Supervision for Parameter-Efficient Video Diffusion Adaptation
authors: Nan Wu, Yee Hung Hong
abstract: Explicit point correspondence is attractive for adapting video generators: it describes how visible surfaces move, but can overwrite the appearance prior learned by a large pretrained model. We study this tension in a 5.01B-parameter text-to-video diffusion transformer. title: Iterate on an LLM, Serve on an SLM
authors: Keegan Wang
abstract: As frontier LLMs gain more capabilities, the cost to run them also goes up. At the same time, small language models (SLMs) also gain more capabilities but have largely been able to keep their cost stable, offering 5-40 times cheaper inference for the narrow, repetitive subtasks that agents decompose work into. title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
authors: Lass Najmuldeen, Seyedhamidreza Mousavi
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. title: Do LLMs differentiate linguistic traits internally?: A layer-wise analysis
authors: Samhita Bollepally, Takashi Yamauchi, Manju Muralee et al.
abstract: Large language models often produce judgments that resemble human responses, but it remains unclear whether they internally capture linguistic nuances such as conventional versus idiomatic meaning. A layer-wise representational analysis was conducted on two equal-sized pre-trained models, Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-3-1B-PT, to examine whether and where these models differentiate linguistic traits from input. title: Can You Trust Your Preference Models? Stackelberg Games for Alignment
authors: Riccardo Formenti, Aditya Agrawal, Vikas Garg
abstract: Language models are frequently aligned to human preferences via imperfect evaluators whose errors can be exploited during optimization. We train policies to search for comparisons on which an evaluator may reverse the underlying preference, providing candidates for additional supervision. Since human preferences are unavailable during policy training, we use disagreement among an ensemble of preference models as a proxy for prediction error. title: Single-Sample Decoding of a Two-Layer Sound-Word Canvas Model for Thai Klon Pad
authors: Worasait Suwannik
abstract: We present a generator of Thai klon pad verse, one stanza from a short topic, and evaluate it against human verse on held-out topics. The generator is a masked language model initialised from WangchanBERTa over a fixed canvas with two layers: a sound layer of pronounced syllables, where rhyme, tone and syllable count are enforced as hard masks, and a word layer of whole words, so that no word is cut into written pieces. title: Predicting how model propensities generalize out of distribution
authors: June Hunter, Lily Wen, Owen Terry et al.
abstract: How do language models generalize from their training data? This is a central challenge for alignment: models reliably learn their training distribution given enough samples, but we want models that behave well when deployed in new contexts. We study out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of propensities. title: FidelityQ: Preserving Predictive Fidelity in Ultra-Low-Bit Language Model Quantization
authors: Yujie Chen, Weiyan Zheng, Yiwu Yao et al.
abstract: Ultra-low-bit scalar quantization offers a regular arithmetic structure for efficient deployment of large language models, but preserving predictive behavior at extreme precision remains challenging: with only a few reconstruction levels, accurate weight representation must translate into consistent predictions from a small calibration set. title: Social Bias in Chinese Large Language Models under Social Media Expressions
authors: Mo Zhou
abstract: Existing Chinese social-bias benchmarks for large language models largely rely on normalized or template-based expressions, leaving the influence of internet slang, emoji, and sarcasm insufficiently examined. Safety alignment may further compress conventional plausibility ratings toward the lower end of the scale. This study constructs 73 paired probes across gender, region, and occupation. title: Relational Semantic Grounding for Test-Time Discovery
authors: Tianle Liu, Gongbo Cheng, Chenggong Ni et al.
abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones from a continuous unlabeled test stream after deployment. Existing TTD methods mainly rely on visual clustering or prototype comparison, and can only assign anonymous labels to discovered classes, leaving them difficult to interpret in open-world applications. title: Uniform Information Density-Based Preference Optimization
authors: Yongyuan Li, Yang Xu
abstract: To enable large language models to generate outputs that align with human preferences, optimization algorithms based on the comparison between chosen and rejected output pairs have been developed and been proven effective. Some recent endeavors have utilized certain linguistically-derived assumptions about the preference pairs to guide the design of more precise optimization directions. title: LLM-based User-Product Relevance Evaluation for Dynamic Product Advertising
authors: Wen Zhang, Xiao Bai, Hsiang-wei Chao et al.
abstract: Dynamic Product Advertising (DPA) retrieval systems are a core component of modern e-commerce advertising; however, their evaluation remains challenging. Conventional offline engagement metrics are limited by sparse, biased feedback, while online evaluation is costly and time-consuming. In this work, we propose a user--product relevance metric for offline evaluation of DPA retrieval systems. title: Scale, Drivers, and Limits of Representational Alignment Across Large Language Models
authors: Jialin Wu, Meenakshi Khosla
abstract: Comparing large language models can reveal shared representational structure and systematic differences between them. However, aggregate similarity measures can obscure how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties support it. We introduce two complementary methods to resolve where models agree and what supports that agreement. title: Only What You've Signed up For: Secure Workflows with Constrained Diffusion Agents
authors: Michael Cardei, Anjun Hu, Chenrui Ma et al.
abstract: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. title: RegExtract: A Benchmark for PFAS Regulatory Information Extraction with LLMs
authors: Defne Circi, Krystelle Lionti, Sarathkrishna Swaminathan et al.
abstract: Extracting structured information from regulatory documents is a critical but challenging task. Relevant facts are scattered across long, legally dense texts, and traceability of extracted facts to their source is essential for verification. title: Swarm Telepathy: Prefill-Free KV-Cache Transfer Across Families
authors: Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Irene Tenison, Yang Zhang et al.
abstract: LLM multi-agent systems split work across agents that communicate through text. An agent summarizes its findings, another agent receives the text. This constrains communication to discrete tokens and costs redundant compute, limiting bandwidth and capabilities of multi-agent systems. Recent works demonstrate KV-cache transfer between LLMs but they either require the LLMs to be within the same family or cannot function across context, thus requiring the receiver to prefill text. title: SkillHorizon: Constructing Long-Horizon Agent Tasks through Skill Composition
authors: Yuxuan Liu, Zhaochen Su, Hangyu Guo et al.
abstract: Long-horizon agents must complete workflows in which later activities depend on earlier outputs and changes to shared state. A key challenge for evaluation is to expand task requirements and their dependencies while keeping tasks executable and outcomes verifiable. We introduce SkillHorizon, a benchmark that constructs long-horizon tasks through skill composition in seven business environments. title: Towards Merging-conditional Backdoor Unalignment against Large Language Models
authors: Yukun Chen, Yidou Chen, Yiming Li et al.
abstract: Model merging has become widely adopted for enhancing the task-specific performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) without additional training. While the specialized model from third-party platforms may undergo safety audits (e.g., backdoor detection), we reveal a novel and critical threat: One-sided Merging-Conditional Backdoor (OMCB). title: TagBO: LLM-Driven Task-Aware Graph Bayesian Optimization for Scientific Discovery
authors: Xinzhe Yuan, Zimu Zeng, Zhuo Chen et al.
abstract: Mixed-variable optimization in scientific discovery often requires exploring large combinatorial spaces under costly experimental evaluations, making sample?efficient Bayesian optimization (BO) essential. However, existing BO methods typ?ically rely on structural descriptors to define similarity among categorical variables, implicitly assuming that structural similarity reflects similarity in task performance. title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models
authors: Yuqiu Deng, Muyun Jiang, Zongpeng Zhang et al.
abstract: EEG foundation models (EFMs) have improved EEG representation learning by transferring knowledge from large-scale multi-subject pretraining to downstream tasks. However, their pretrained embeddings often retain substantial subject-related variation, placing an additional burden on the downstream classifier, especially in cross-subject settings. title: Verifiable Retrieval for Legal Reasoning through Structure-driven Knowledge Graph
authors: Ibrahim Siddig, Sviatoslav Tugeev, Munir Georges
abstract: Any automation within reliability-critical contexts such as medicine or law has to be transparent and verifiable. Despite their advantages, current LLM-based systems do not meet these requirements due to their inherent black-box nature. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) attempts to ground the generative process in the relevant interpretable documents, thereby reducing the risk of AI 'hallucinations' and potentially enabling verification of the initial generation context. title: SmartSalesBench: A Resistance-Aware Multi-Turn Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Sales Agents
authors: P N Bhargav Teja, Velpula Lokesh Reddy, Madhu Basumata et al.
abstract: We present SmartSalesBench, the first multi-turn conversational benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) sales agents against psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas. Existing task-oriented dialogue benchmarks assume cooperative users and measure task completion; SmartSalesBench inverts this assumption, placing agents against personas programmed to resist and challenge across conversations of up to twenty turns. title: Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training
authors: Chenxu Zhang, Yaorui Shi, Wenlong Zhang et al.
abstract: Training long-horizon language model agents requires assigning credit to intermediate decisions from sparse terminal feedback. Within a finite group of sibling rollouts, useful action comparisons depend on their context, evidence for both alternatives, and how that evidence enters learning. We propose Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization (MCGPO), a procedure for constructing weighted action preferences from already collected trajectories. title: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models
authors: Ivan Moloshnikov, Dmitry Kunitsyn, Alexander Sboev et al.
abstract: Many machine learning approaches are two-level: an expert selects a class of methods, within this class the choice of key components is critical and usually manual. This paper addresses the automatic tuning of these components and proposes a framework transferable across models of different nature. The multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework has three roles---analyst, coder, and recorder~---with an experiment log and a sandboxed execution environment. title: Humanize Olympiad Agents: A Multi-Session Workflow for Olympiad Problem Solving with Solve, Review, Wiki, Verify
authors: Zhengyang Zhang, Jing Xiong, Hongzhou Lin et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly improving on long-horizon scientific and olympiad tasks. Recent systems have produced a Lean-formalized resolution of the Navier--Stokes problem and autonomous solutions to four open questions in the Erdős Conjectures database. Yet neither system releases both its underlying model and complete inference stack. title: Proactive Agentic Orchestration
authors: Xueyang Feng, Chaozhuo Li, Xiaohe Bo et al.
abstract: Agentic orchestration delegates tasks to sub-agents with independent contexts, providing a key path to extending the effective execution horizon of large language model agents. However, existing orchestration methods face two limitations: in execution, current methods fix sub-agents' goals and harnesses at creation time, limiting their adaptability to dynamic real-world environments; in optimization, sparse and delayed feedback constrains effective learning of the orchestration policy. title: Agentic Large Language Models
authors: Max van Duijn, Michiel van der Meer, Aske Plaat et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm. Their ability to communicate with us in our own language, and to reason about our world, has made them a favorite tool for writing, answering questions, and much more. Their answers already influence our decisions and our actions. What would happen if LLMs themselves could act in the world directly? What would happen if LLMs could interact with each other? title: Rollout-Time Intervention: Unlocking Agentic Reinforcement Learning Beyond Policy Limits
authors: Chen Xi, Ding Ruixue, Wang Zhigaoyuan et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) agents, enabling stronger reasoning, planning, and tool-use in interactive environments. However, existing agent RL methods remain fundamentally constrained by an on-policy reasoning bottleneck: when tasks exceed the model's current capability boundary, effective trajectories become extremely sparse and training often collapses. authors: Sunghwan Kim, Deogyong Kim, Sangam Lee et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming direct users of the open web. As they take on increasingly complex and information-intensive tasks, effective web access is becoming a core capability for agentic problem solving. Existing approaches have advanced agentic web access through different access models, including search-augmented agents, browser-based agents, and, more recently, filesystem-based agents.
